soil-bio-081.title: Dwarf forests, where poor soil grows miniature trees
soil-bio-081.text: On Mount Hamiguitan in the Philippines, 6,834 hectares of forest grow in miniature. It is the largest known pygmy forest in the country and possibly the world. A dwarf forest, also called an elfin or pygmy forest, is an uncommon ecosystem of small trees, home to small animals such as rodents and lizards. Most grow at high elevations, where the air is humid but the soil is poor. The two main types are coastal temperate and montane tropical. In tropical mountains the trees reach only 5–8 m, with shallow roots and abundant epiphytes, plants that grow perched on other plants. High winds largely set their height.

soil-bio-069.title: Soil-borne pathogens, the enemies waiting below the crop
soil-bio-069.text: Some of a plant's worst enemies wait in the ground beneath it. A soil-borne pathogen is a disease-causing agent that lives both in soil and in a plant host, and it tends to infect healthy plants grown in that soil. Common examples are Fusarium, Pythium, Rhizoctonia, Phytophthora, Verticillium, Rhizopus, Thielaviopsis and nematodes such as Meloidogyne. Many are fungi, even though other soil fungi are helpful partners of plants. Their propagules are the spores and fragments that spread them. Chemicals released by plants can stir them to germinate in the soil around a seedling's lower stem. They then start the stem rots that cause damping-off, the collapse of young seedlings. Monoculture and chemical fertilization often bring these diseases, along with acidification and degradation that lower productivity. Growers have several defenses. Fallowing disrupts pathogens by removing their hosts for a while. Heating the soil with sunlight, {{ref:soil-agri-034}}, kills or badly weakens many. Disease-suppressive soils inhibit them, and teas brewed from {{ref:soil-fert-028}} suppress them too. Growing roots in substrates instead of soil, as {{ref:soil-fert-167}} does, eliminates soil-borne diseases and pests altogether.

soil-bio-045.title: Worm casts, the soil that has passed through a worm
soil-bio-045.text: A small coil of soil on a lawn is the end of a digestive journey. A worm cast is a pile, coil or pellet of soil or sand that burrowing worms push out at the surface. A {{ref:soil-bio-040}} swallows soil along with its microbes and {{ref:soil-found-045}}. Digestion breaks up mineral particles and partly breaks down that dead material, and the rest leaves through the burrow. Casts often hold more plant-available nutrients than the soil around them, and they build stable aggregates, the crumbs that give soil its structure. On lawns and grasslands they are read as a sign of active, healthy soil. On beaches and tidal flats, burrowing polychaete worms leave coiled casts like spaghetti.

soil-bio-035.title: Heat, water and nitrogen set the pace of soil breathing
soil-bio-035.text: Warm soil breathes faster, but only up to a point. Three non-living factors chiefly set how fast carbon in soil is respired to CO2. They are temperature, moisture and nitrogen. {{ref:soil-bio-033}} rises exponentially with temperature to a maximum, then falls to zero as enzymes fail. Roots start to shut down above 35 °C. Microbes divide the range among them. Cryophiles work best below 20 °C, mesophiles between 20 and 40 °C, and thermophiles above 40 °C, so mixed communities respire over a broad span. Moisture traces a hill: respiration is low when dry, peaks at intermediate moisture and falls when water shuts out oxygen. Nitrogen costs roots energy. Taking in nitrate costs 0.4 units of CO2, and reducing it costs 2. Nitrogen-rich litter also decomposes faster.

soil-bio-036.title: Putting a lid on the soil to measure its breath
soil-bio-036.text: To measure how fast soil breathes, researchers put a lid on it. A closed chamber is sealed over the soil, and the flux comes from how fast CO2 builds up over a few minutes, using F=bV/A. Longer runs underestimate it, because some CO2 is stored in the soil instead. Open systems pump fresh air through the chamber and read the flux at equilibrium. Basal respiration is measured with nothing added; substrate-induced respiration adds nutrients and sugars. Stable carbon isotopes reveal where the CO2 comes from. Swapping C3 and C4 crops, plants with two different kinds of photosynthesis, or spraying C4 cane sugar, tells old carbon from new and microbial respiration from root respiration.

soil-bio-037.title: How a changing planet is changing soil's breath
soil-bio-037.text: Soil breathing shifts with every change people make to air and land. Free air CO2 enrichment (FACE) studies raise CO2 over open plots. Elevated CO2 boosted soil respiration through more roots and microbial activity, by up to 40.6% in sweetgum and poplar forests. Warming may hit hardest in the Arctic. There, thawing permafrost turns aerobic, and its large carbon stores are respired much faster. Rainfall matters too. Dry soils burst into respiration after rain and slow as they dry, so more frequent, intense rain should raise respiration sharply in arid lands. Nitrogen fertilization since the Green Revolution has boosted plant growth, root respiration and root biomass, and soil respiration along with them.

soil-bio-034.title: Roots, microbes and animals: who breathes out soil CO2
soil-bio-034.text: Roughly half the CO2 rising from soil comes from roots. Root respiration accounts for approximately half of {{ref:soil-bio-033}}, though values range from 10 to 90% with plant type and conditions. The rest comes from the organisms around them. Up to 20% of the carbon a plant captures in photosynthesis leaks into the soil from roots, and bacteria decompose most of it. Fungi partnered with roots also respire sugars the plant gives them. Most of the CO2 comes from the TCA cycle of cellular respiration. Fermentation, which works without oxygen, adds more in the oxygen-poor soil right around roots. Soil animals contribute by grazing bacteria and fungi and by fragmenting litter, which exposes more surface to microbes.

soil-bio-067.title: Bacteria that turn loose soil into stone
soil-bio-067.text: Bacteria can glue sand grains together with crystals of their own making. Microbiologically induced calcite precipitation is a biogeochemical process in which microbes cause calcium carbonate to precipitate within the soil. It is a form of {{ref:soil-bio-063}}. The main microbes able to induce it are photosynthetic cyanobacteria and microalgae, sulfate-reducing bacteria and some species that cycle nitrogen. Bacteria can trigger it by breaking down {{ref:soil-fert-021}}, by {{ref:soil-fert-108}}, by sulfate production or by iron reduction. Autotrophic pathways use up carbon dioxide, while heterotrophic ones run through the cycling of nitrogen and sulfur. The first route, ureolysis, shows the chemistry step by step. A microbial enzyme, urease, splits this nitrogen compound into ammonium and carbonate. Hydroxide ions formed along the way raise the pH and shift bicarbonate to carbonate. That carbonate meets calcium and drops out as calcium carbonate crystals. The process feeds itself. A first layer of calcite makes bacteria cling more strongly to the soil surface, so further layers build up. The carbonate can form as calcite, aragonite or vaterite, in that order of usual stability. Such biological precipitation goes back to the Precambrian. Proposed uses include repairing cracks in concrete, preventing its corrosion and making biogrout. The process can also lock away radionuclides and heavy metals. They are trapped by co-precipitation into the calcite lattice, and binding to the precipitate makes lead in soil less available. Its use to strengthen sand is {{ref:soil-bio-068}}.

soil-bio-019.title: Soil zoology, the science of animals underfoot
soil-bio-019.text: In Russia in the 1940s, Mercury Ghilarov built a science around the animals underfoot. Soil zoology, or pedozoology, studies animals that live wholly or partly in the soil. Ghilarov noticed that the smaller soil organisms are, the more numerous they are. He also suggested that soil may have been the transitional environment between life in water and life on land. The English term was apparently first used at a 1955 conference of soil zoologists at the University of Nottingham. The field has practical value. Studying how {{ref:soil-bio-020}} interact can help farmers cut chemical use through {{ref:soil-agri-054}}.

soil-bio-066.title: When a living thing makes a crystal, is it a mineral?
soil-bio-066.text: Is a crystal grown by a living thing a mineral? The geological definition of a mineral normally excludes compounds found only in living beings. Yet calcite is often biogenic, and organisms make hydroxylapatite, which also occurs in rocks. As of December 2020, the International Mineralogical Association, the recognized standard body, had accepted 5,650 official mineral species out of 5,862 proposed or traditional ones. Its decision to exclude biogenic crystalline substances divides geologists and mineralogists, and the dispute remains open. Lowenstam noted in 1981 that organisms form some minerals that cannot form inorganically. Skinner, in 2005, counted any element or compound formed through biogeochemical processes as a mineral, amorphous or crystalline. Mineral-forming microbes live on nearly every rock, soil and particle surface, down to at least 1,600 meters below the sea floor.

soil-bio-065.title: Geomycology: fungi that build and break minerals
soil-bio-065.text: Fungi quietly do geology. Geomycology is the study of the part fungi play in geological processes, including forming, transforming and dissolving minerals. Fungi deposit minerals on an organic matrix, such as a protein, that gives crystals a place to start. Proteins they secrete control the size and shape of the carbonate minerals they precipitate. Using organic phosphorus, fungi can even precipitate uranium-bearing phosphate minerals and gather them in their mycelium. Aspergillus niger and Paecilomyces javanicus tolerate uranium. Fungi also break minerals down, joining in {{ref:soil-found-052}}. The main culprits are strains that produce oxalic acid: Aspergillus niger, Serpula himantioides and Trametes versicolor corrode apatite and galena.

soil-bio-064.title: Three degrees of control in living mineral-making
soil-bio-064.text: Living things build minerals with very different degrees of control. One scheme, following a 2009 framework by Dupraz and colleagues, sorts {{ref:soil-bio-063}} into three kinds. In the biologically controlled kind, the cells of one organism fully control the crystals' shape, growth, composition and location. Mollusc and brachiopod shells are built this way. In the biologically induced kind, microbial metabolism creates chemical conditions that favor mineral growth on an organic matrix the microbes secrete. Stromatolites and other microbial mats form like this. In the biologically influenced kind, abiotic processes such as evaporation or degassing set the chemistry, while a microbial organic matrix still shapes the crystals. The terms have no standardized definitions, and their use varies widely.

soil-bio-071.title: Ammonia fungi, which fruit where nitrogen floods the soil
soil-bio-071.text: Where an animal dies or leaves its dung in a forest, a particular set of fungi follows. Ammonia fungi fruit quickly and germinate readily when ammonia or other nitrogen-rich material makes the soil alkaline. Heavy additions of ammonia or {{ref:soil-fert-021}} do the same, raising the pH of soil litter to 8–10 and interrupting the recycling of nutrients. The fungi thrive until the soil reverts, which takes up to 2 years for soil ammonia, helped by late-phase fungi. Most live in temperate forests on well-rotted wood, plant debris or dung. They are most active in the O horizon, then the A and B horizons. They help maintain the cycling of nitrogen, and some are predators: Laccaria bicolor catches and kills springtails.

soil-bio-059.title: Acid mine drainage, sulfuric acid brewed by microbes
soil-bio-059.text: Streams below some mines run at pH 2–3. Acid mine drainage is the acid runoff made when lithotrophic microbes in mining areas oxidize pyrite and other reduced sulfur minerals to sulfate. The acid-loving bacterium Acidithiobacillus ferrooxidans, for example, uses iron sulfide to generate sulfuric acid, which drains from the mine with runoff. It changes the chemistry of groundwater and streams and may endanger plant and animal populations downstream. This is {{ref:soil-bio-057}} on an industrial scale. The same activity runs far more modestly in nature: in soil and talus, on glacier beds, on stone buildings and monuments, and in the deep subsurface.

soil-bio-058.title: How microbes living on bare rock start a soil
soil-bio-058.text: On bare rock, soil formation begins with microbes that can live on stone. Rock-colonizing lithotrophs, cyanobacteria above all, take that first step. Cyanobacteria are nitrogen-fixing photolithotrophs. They take energy from sunlight and use inorganic nutrients from rock as reductants, the electron donors their chemistry needs. That lets them grow on native, nutrient-poor rock and leave behind organic material that other organisms can then colonize. Colonization can start the breakdown of organic compounds, a primary factor in soil genesis. The mechanism is thought to have helped shape the early biological Earth, and it makes cyanobacteria classic {{ref:soil-found-085}}.

soil-bio-086.title: Oribatid mites, the slow-living shredders of forest litter
soil-bio-086.text: About 12,000 species of oribatid mites have been described, and the true total may run from 60,000 to 120,000. Also called moss or beetle mites, these slow-living mites are the most prevalent arthropods in forest soils. They measure 0.2 to 1.4 millimeters. They eat living and dead plant and fungal material, lichens and carrion, and none is parasitic. That diet makes them essential for breaking down organic debris and distributing fungi. Like earthworms, they speed decay. Unlike many earthworms, they do not mix it with mineral matter. Some mine conifer needles from the inside. They develop slowly and have few offspring, taking months to two years to mature in temperate forest soils. They are densest in forests with thick organic layers.

soil-bio-010.title: Counting soil life by reading its DNA
soil-bio-010.text: Most soil microbes have never been cultured and remain undescribed, so measuring the diversity of soil life is hard. The answer, increasingly, is to read DNA instead of growing cells. Next-generation sequencing of DNA extracted directly from the soil is opening {{ref:soil-bio-008}} to study. Omics approaches for microbes are advancing fast. Metagenomics reads the genes of a whole community, metatranscriptomics its active genes and proteomics its proteins. Metaphenomics has been proposed to add environmental constraints. Much remains unknown. A 2020 FAO report found major gaps in knowledge about biodiversity in soils.

soil-bio-028.title: Bottom-up control: feed the base and the web swells
soil-bio-028.text: Feed the base of a food web and the whole web grows. In bottom-up control, the biomass, abundance or diversity of higher levels depends on resources from lower levels. The evidence is correlation: consumers rise and fall with their resources. On land, the biomass of herbivores and detritivores rises with primary productivity, the rate at which plants make new growth. In the {{ref:soil-bio-025}} the chain is easy to follow. More productivity means more leaf litter, then more bacteria and fungi, more nematodes that eat them, and more mites and predatory nematodes. The whole web swells.

soil-bio-032.title: The external rumen: animals that let microbes cook their food
soil-bio-032.text: An isopod kept from eating its own feces can die. That odd fact reveals an external rumen: a partnership in which litter-eating animals let microbes enrich their fecal pellets outside the body, then eat the pellets again. Isopods and other litter transformers excrete pellets that are moister and richer in nutrients than the soil around them. Bacteria and fungi colonize those pellets. On nutrient-poor litter, the microbes turn them into better food. Fungi do the same for wood-eaters. They enrich nutritionally scarce dead wood, so xylophages, the animals that eat wood, can develop and speed its decay. Standard food webs miss such partnerships, because they emphasize competition and predation.

soil-bio-031.title: Funnels, cores and lamps: getting animals out of soil
soil-bio-031.text: Counting soil animals starts with getting them out of the soil. Samples are often taken with a metal core. Large animals such as earthworms can be picked out by hand, but that is impossible for nematodes and small arthropods. A dry Berlese funnel drives microarthropods downward, away from light and heat, into a collecting vial. A wet Baermann funnel collects nematodes, which sink because they cannot swim. Microbes need other tricks. They are characterized by their respiration, by genetic profiling of extracted cell components, or by biomass estimated before and after fumigation.

soil-bio-029.title: Do soil predators rule the web from the top?
soil-bio-029.text: Do the hunters in soil control the hunted? In top-down control, consumers higher in a food web set the abundance, diversity or biomass of the levels below. Its signature is the trophic cascade, in which predators affect organisms at least two links down. Whether cascades matter on land is actively debated. In soil they occur in the bacterial and fungal channels, but they may be infrequent. Omnivory, dormancy and the spatial separation of predator and prey all damp top-down effects. Soil webs are also donor controlled: decomposers cannot change how fast litter falls. Added predators or parasites can still matter. A nematode that kills insects, {{ref:soil-bio-083}}, killed root-eating ghost moth caterpillars and so protected bush lupine. That is the principle behind biological control.

soil-bio-030.title: Why tangled soil food webs hold together
soil-bio-030.text: Theory once said that complexity makes food webs unstable. May's models, built on randomly linked community matrices, predicted exactly that, and soil webs were long thought simple. The random matrices drew much criticism. Soil food webs did not fit the predictions. Their long, complex, omnivorous chains resisted drying, freezing and fumigation. Several features promote that stability: many weak interactions, donor control, the buffering of soil structure, and dormancy in organisms such as bacteria. Donor control is the same limit that weakens {{ref:soil-bio-029}}. One practice works against stability. Nitrogen-containing fertilizers reduce it because they acidify soil.
